text: Given nums and target, put a plus or a minus in front of every number and concatenate them into an expression. Return how many different expressions evaluate to target.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — every number gets a sign, none are skipped, and the order is fixed. So I'm counting sign assignments, not orderings. What are the bounds?
At most twenty numbers, each between zero and one thousand, and the total sum is at most one thousand. Target is between minus one thousand and one thousand.

Two things I want to pin down. Can nums contain zeros? That matters — a zero can take plus zero or minus zero, which are two distinct expressions with the same value, so each zero should double the count.
Good question — yes, zeros are allowed, and you're right that they double.
Let me run through an example. Five ones with target three gives five: pick four pluses and one minus, and there are five choices of which one is negative.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. The honest baseline first: brute force over all two to the n sign choices is about a million here — that actually passes, but only because n is at most twenty; it doesn't see the structure. The reframe: assigning signs is the same as splitting into two piles, the plus pile with sum P and the minus pile with sum N. P minus N is target, P plus N is the total. Add the two and N cancels: P is target plus total, over two. And this is the part that matters — P is a constant I can compute, not a variable to search over. So the question becomes how many subsets sum to P. This problem reminds me of a zero-one knapsack, in its counting form — subset sum, but counting ways instead of asking yes or no.
Nice. Any inputs where that formula breaks?

Yes, two — and I'd guard both before allocating anything. One: if the total is less than the absolute value of target, it's unreachable — the best I can do is all-plus or all-minus. Worse, P goes negative: a single one with target minus five gives P of minus two, and allocating a vector of size minus one blows up. Two: if target plus total is odd, P isn't an integer, so it's impossible. This one is nastier because it fails silently — integer division truncates and you get a plausible wrong answer. Two, two with target one: every plus-or-minus two, plus-or-minus two is even, so the answer is zero, but without the guard you'd compute P equals two and return two.

Here's the plan. One: compute the total, and return zero if either guard fires. Two: set P to target plus total over two, and seed dp of zero with one, for the empty subset. Three: for each number, sweep s from P down to that number, adding dp of s minus num into dp of s, and return dp of P. Two notes. The skeleton is identical to the yes-or-no subset-sum knapsack — the only change is that OR becomes plus: can I uses OR, how many uses plus. And the descending inner loop is what keeps it zero-one rather than unbounded. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Sounds good. What about the zeros you mentioned — special case?
Let me think… No — it falls out for free. When num is zero, the update adds dp of s to itself, so every cell doubles. That's exactly the doubling we want. No special case, no extra code.

Alright, let me code this up. Guards first, then P, then the one-dimensional table with a descending inner loop. The line that's easy to get wrong is the guard: the parity check has to sit next to the range check, before the division, because the division never complains — it just truncates. That's order n times P time and order P space. The check that skips zero cells is just a micro-optimization — correctness doesn't depend on it.
You used unsigned int. Why? Is that necessary?

That's a fair challenge — it's not necessary here. Let me bound the answer: it counts sign assignments, and there are only two to the n of those, so with n at most twenty the answer is at most about a million — around point zero five percent of the int maximum. Every intermediate dp cell is also a subset count, so it's bounded the same way. Int is fine; the unsigned is harmless insurance, not load-bearing. It would be load-bearing in a counting problem where intermediate counts genuinely exceed the int maximum — there int is signed overflow, which is undefined behaviour, whereas unsigned wraps well-defined. The right habit is to bound the answer first, then pick the type — not reach for unsigned out of superstition.

Let's dry-run five ones with target three. Total is five, the sum is eight, even, so P is four; expected five. The row that decides it is the fifth one: dp of four picks up dp of three, which is four, and becomes five. That matches. The rows are Pascal's triangle — makes sense, since each update is literally the binomial recurrence. Corner cases: one, two, three with target zero gives two. One, zero with target one gives two, because the zero doubles. Two, two with target one gives zero, from the parity guard. And a single one with target two gives zero, from the range guard.

Time is order n times P, about twenty times a thousand, twenty thousand, and space is order P. Versus a million for brute force — fifty times fewer operations, and more importantly it stops being exponential in n. Oh, one more thing — this is pseudo-polynomial: the cost tracks the magnitude of P, not its bit-length. If values could be a billion with n still at most twenty, the table becomes unbuildable and I'd switch to meet-in-the-middle: enumerate the signed sums of each half, hash one side, and look up the complement. That's two to the n over two. Small n with big values means meet-in-the-middle; big n with small values means knapsack.

Strong pass. Three things stood out. You derived P as target plus total over two, and identified that it's a constant, which is the whole problem. You found both guards yourself and knew the parity one fails silently — that's the bug most people ship. And when I pushed on unsigned, you bounded the answer instead of defending the habit. Good work.
